{{Short description|Generalization of a fixed point}}
{{About|the technical mathematical concept of coincidence|numerical curiosities|mathematical coincidence}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''coincidence point''' (or simply '''coincidence''') of two [[function (mathematics)|functions]] is a point in their common [[domain of a function|domain]] having the same image.

Formally, given two functions
<math display="block">f,g \colon X \rightarrow Y</math>
we say that a point ''x'' in ''X'' is a ''coincidence point'' of ''f'' and ''g'' if ''f''(''x'') = ''g''(''x'').<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Granas | first1 = Andrzej
 | last2 = Dugundji | first2 = James
 | doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-21593-8
 | isbn = 0-387-00173-5
 | location = New York
 | mr = 1987179
 | page = xvi+690
 | publisher = [[Springer-Verlag]]
 | series = Springer Monographs in Mathematics
 | title = Fixed point theory
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=4_iJAoLSq3cC&pg=PA531
 | year = 2003| url-access = subscription
 }}.</ref>

Coincidence theory (the study of coincidence points) is, in most settings, a generalization of [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] theory, the study of points ''x'' with ''f''(''x'') = ''x''. Fixed point theory is the special case obtained from the above by letting ''X = Y'' and taking ''g'' to be the [[identity function]].

Just as fixed point theory has its [[fixed-point theorem]]s, there are [[theorem]]s that guarantee the existence of coincidence points for pairs of functions. Notable among them, in the setting of [[manifold]]s, is the [[Lefschetz fixed-point theorem|Lefschetz coincidence theorem]], which is typically known only in its [[special case]] formulation for fixed points.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Górniewicz | first = Lech
 | contribution = On the Lefschetz coincidence theorem
 | doi = 10.1007/BFb0092179
 | mr = 643002
 | pages = 116–139
 | publisher = Springer, Berlin-New York
 | series = Lecture Notes in Math.
 | title = Fixed point theory (Sherbrooke, Que., 1980)
 | volume = 886
 | year = 1981| isbn = 978-3-540-11152-8
 }}.</ref>

Coincidence points, like fixed points, are today studied using many tools from [[mathematical analysis]] and [[topology]]. An [[Equaliser (mathematics)|equaliser]] is a generalization of the coincidence set.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Staecker | first = P. Christopher
 | arxiv = 1008.2154
 | doi = 10.1016/j.topol.2011.05.032
 | issue = 13
 | journal = Topology and Its Applications
 | mr = 2812471
 | pages = 1615–1625
 | title = Nielsen equalizer theory
 | volume = 158
 | year = 2011| s2cid = 54999598
 }}.</ref>
